Reading the curves
Judge the trend over training, not a single snapshot
Underfit

traintest
Underfitting

Train error
Stays high
Keeps falling, often to 0
Test error
High, tracking train error
Rises while train error improves
Cause
High bias: the model class cannot express the solution
High variance: the model is too flexible for the data
Fix
A more capable or better-suited model class
More data, regularization (dropout, weight decay), early stopping, less capacity
DEFINITION TO CARRY FORWARD
A model generalizes when it has low error on a held-out test set drawn from the same distribution as training.
A high test error alone is ambiguous; the direction it moves tells you which problem you have.

How big is this class?
A wide enough network can approximate any continuous function on a bounded input space.
Universal approximation: Cybenko 1989; Hornik et al. 1989
And the data is small by comparison
Our residual MLP: 4.7 × 10⁵ parameters, 8.0 × 10³ training images.

Where in the model space do you expect a trained deep neural net to be?
AFits the training data, not the test data
BFits both the training and the test data
CFits neither

Yet on real labels, it works
4.7 × 10⁵
parameters
8.0 × 10³
training images: about 58 parameters per image
96%
test accuracy, with 100% training accuracy
The answer to the prediction is B: out of a class that covers almost everything, training landed among the models that also fit the test data.
Most models in this class that fit the training data would fail the test. Training somehow avoided them.
Far more parameters than training images, and it still generalizes.
But why?

A hypothesis: the data is too hard to memorize
Maybe the class is smaller in practice than it looks on the map
label 3
label 8
label 1
label 0
label 4
label 0
6 of the 8,000 training images. Each is 784 pixel values, and every one must be mapped to its label.
HYPOTHESIS
Storing 8,000 separate image-to-label answers is too hard for this network. The only way it can fit the training data is to find patterns shared across many images, and shared patterns also work on new images.
If it is true
The huge class is not really a problem: in practice the network can only reach models that capture structure, so it lands in B.
A hypothesis is only useful if some experiment could prove it wrong.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
A test: shuffle the labels
?
Same 8,000 images, same number of each label; only the pairing of image and label is scrambled
true 3 given 9
true 8 given 7
true 1 given 8
true 0 given 3
true 4 given 7
true 0 given 4
Why this test tells us something
No rule links image to label anymore: the shuffled labels match the true ones on 9.6% of images, which is chance.
That leaves training accuracy as a pure measure of memorization: can the class store 8,000 arbitrary answers?
Two possible outcomes
Training accuracy stays low: the class cannot memorize. Its limited size could be what makes it generalize.
Training accuracy reaches ~100%: the class can memorize anything. Its size cannot be what makes it generalize.
Predict before the next slide: which outcome will we see?
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
It can memorize noise
Same MLP, same 8,000 images; one run with true labels, one with labels shuffled at random
100%
75%
50%

0%
0
20

60
epoch
true labels: train 100%, test 96%
random labels: train
random labels: test ≈ chance
Solid: training accuracy · dashed: test accuracy · dotted: chance (10%)
99%
of 8,000 meaningless labels memorized by epoch 60. Test accuracy: 9.7%, chance level.
Memorizing noise takes longer: 70% at epoch 10, where true labels are already at 99%. But it gets there.
Standard image networks memorize random labels on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, and even pure-noise images on CIFAR-10.
Zhang et al. (2017), "Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization"
The hypothesis was wrong. So, why do deep nets generalize?

Class: p = 50 hidden units
Hypothesis 2: maybe the classical picture is wrong
An experiment where we control the size of the class: one hidden layer, more and more hidden units
Each added hidden unit adds new functions the model can express: the chosen class grows to take in more of the space.
The model
The first layer is random and never trained. Only W is fit, exactly, by ordinary least squares (OLS): the optimal linear combination of the p hidden units.
Classical picture: training picks any model that fits. A bigger class holds more models that fit the training data but fail the test, so past some size test error only rises.
Hypothesis 2: the classical picture is wrong. Training does not pick arbitrarily, so test error could fall even as the class grows.

The classical assumption
Training picks any model that fits. More parameters mean more ways to fit badly, so past the sweet spot test error only gets worse.
What actually happens
Test error spikes at p = n, then falls below the classical best: 17.0% → 8.2%.
Belkin et al. (2019); in deep nets, by width and by training time: Nakkiran et al. (2019)
QUESTION
Past p = n, every model fits the training data perfectly. So why does test error go down?
The classical assumption is wrong: training does not pick uniformly among the models that fit.

Yet training keeps landing on them. Test error falls as the class grows.

The optimization method guides the selection

At p = n exactly one set of weights fits all 1,000 digits. To hit every point it must be huge: norm 1,041, test error 88%.
Past p = n infinitely many weight settings fit exactly. Starting from zero, a weight only grows or shrinks away from zero if that helps performance, so training ends at the smallest-weight fit.
More hidden units make an even smaller fit available: norm 2.7 at p = 10,000, smoother, and test error down to 8.2%.
No penalty term anywhere, yet gradient descent chooses. This is implicit regularization. Ridgeless least squares: Hastie et al. (2022); Bartlett et al. (2020).
Starting from zero, training prefers small-weight solutions. But what about a deep net with random initialization?

Arpit et al. (2017); coherent gradients: Chatterjee (2020); GPT-3: Brown et al. (2020)
EPOCH 1
92% of correctly labeled digits fit, but only 2% of wrongly labeled ones: it predicts the true digit.
EPOCH 3
Test accuracy peaks at 92.6%. Stop here (early stopping) and the noise is never memorized.
EPOCH 60
Wrong labels memorized (99%); test falls to 81%.
Correctly labeled 7s all push the weights the same way, so their gradients add up. A mislabeled digit pushes alone.
Used at scale: large language models are typically trained for about one pass over their data, so most examples are seen once. GPT-3 saw its main web corpus 0.44 times.
Gradient descent follows loud, coherent gradients first. Stop early and the noise is never fit.

1
Many models fit. A deep net can fit the training data countless ways, even pure noise.
2
Training picks one. No penalty decides, so the procedure does: architecture, initialization, optimizer.
3
It picks a simple one. Linear case: the smallest weights. Deep nets: shared structure before noise (after epoch 1, 92% of correctly labeled digits fit vs 2% of mislabeled).
4
Simple fits tend to fit the test data too, when test digits come from the same distribution.
Still debated: optimizer or architecture? Full-batch gradient descent can match SGD (Geiping et al. 2022), and even randomly sampled networks that fit tend to generalize (Chiang et al. 2023).
BUT SIMPLE BY WHOSE STANDARD?
Nothing in this preference says a 7 moved three pixels is still a 7. Let's test it.
Generalization comes from which fit training picks, not how many fits the class contains.

Data augmentation: teaching invariance
For failures along a known, systematic axis: shift, crop, rotation, scale, flip, color

What it does
Each time an image is drawn for a batch, apply a random transformation and keep the label. One 7 becomes every shifted 7.
What it says
"The label does not change under this transformation." An invariance, written into the data instead of the model.
When to use it
When you can name the axis a model fails on. Each axis is its own transformation, taught separately.
Shown: one real test 7 under eight random translations, pad 3 and re-crop (±3 px on each axis).
Augmentation encodes an invariance through the data.

Proposal: add random horizontal flips
?
Flips are a standard augmentation for photos. Each training digit below, mirrored left to right:
a 7 flipped
a 3 flipped
a 4 flipped
a 8 flipped
QUESTION
Train every digit with its label, sometimes flipped. Is this augmentation appropriate?
Proposal: add random horizontal flips
?
Flips are a standard augmentation for photos. Each training digit below, mirrored left to right:
a 7 not a 7
a 3 not a 3
a 4 not a 4
a 8 still an 8
QUESTION
Train every digit with its label, sometimes flipped. Is this augmentation appropriate?
No. A flipped digit is not the same digit. A mirrored 3 is not a 3, and a mirrored 7 or 4 is no digit at all. Augmentation claims the label survives; here it does not. An 8 happens to survive, but one rule has to hold for every class.
Contrast: on CIFAR-10 a mirrored cat is still a cat and a mirrored truck still a truck, so flips are standard there.
© 2026 Dr. Jesse Roberts
The catch: how many training images is that?
A shifted, shrunken, slightly rotated 7 is still a 7, so the axes must be covered in combination
Axis
Settings
Count
Original
MNIST training set
60,000
× Shift (crop)
−3 to +3 px, each axis (7 × 7)
× 49
× Scale
0.8× to 1.2×, steps of 0.1
× 5
× Rotation
−15° to +15°, steps of 5° (small only: 180° turns a 6 into a 9)
× 7
Total
1,715 versions of every digit
1.0 × 10⁸
Combinations multiply, they don't add. Add 3 stroke widths and it is 3.1 × 10⁸. Sampling one random version per image each epoch avoids storing them, but the model still has to see enough of this space: many more epochs.
What else it costs
Capacity spent on copies. The MLP still stores each feature separately at every position, size and angle it was shown.
Only the range shown. Trained on ±3 px: 94% at 3 px, 60% at 6 px. Trained on 0.8–1.2×: 87% at 1.4×.
One axis at a time. Every invariance you name is another factor in the count.
Augmentation works, but it teaches by showing every case rather than knowing the rule.

What this means for your project
Residual MLP on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet: no convolutions, no extra data
ALLOWED
Data augmentation: it does not count as adding data. Expect it to be your biggest lever on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.
TRY THIS WEEK
Run today's shift plot on your own MNIST model.
Compare train and test curves on CIFAR-10: is test error rising?
Add random crops and re-run both.
How far can MLPs go? Bachmann, Anagnostidis & Hofmann (NeurIPS 2023), "Scaling MLPs: A Tale of Inductive Bias": plain MLPs reach 95% on CIFAR-10, but only with large-scale pretraining and heavy augmentation, which this project rules out. Read it for how much compute it takes, not as a target.
On natural images, augmentation is how an MLP rules out solutions that should be systematically excluded.
